turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning, Mrs Pretorius. Come sit. What's been bothering you?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, doctor, where do I start. The legs, hey. But first, did you see the robot on Voortrekker is out again? We sat in the bakkie for ages.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's here about the swelling, doctor. I'm Lindi, I stay in and I do the tablets.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, Lindi knows. My ankles are like pudding. The shoes from my sister's wedding don't go on. Shame.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long have the ankles been like that?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Since... oh, two weeks. No, wait, it's longer. Six weeks, I'd say, after the church bazaar.
[SEG0007] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It's more than that. Closer to two months. I noticed when I was washing her feet at the beginning of last month, and it's worse now.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): All right. I'll put it down as somewhere between six weeks and two months, since the two of you don't quite agree, and there's no firm date.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): And the neighbour's dog, you know, he barks the whole night. I was telling Lindi...
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll come back to the dog. Any shortness of breath?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Nee, my chest is fine. I don't get short of breath.
[SEG0012] person_3 (CAREGIVER): But yesterday at the gate...
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): That was the hill, man. Anyway the dog belongs to Mr Abbas next door, and his bakkie blocks our...
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mrs Pretorius, the breathing.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, ja. When I walk to the gate I have to stop and hold the wall. Not in the house.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any pain in the chest while that's happening?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain. Not once.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): And at night, do you wake up gasping, or do you sleep flat all right?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): I sleep like a log, doctor. Flat, two pillows, no problem. The dog wakes me, not my chest.
[SEG0020] person_3 (CAREGIVER): That's not true, sorry. Three nights this week she sat up on the side of the bed, breathing hard. I heard her from the passage.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, Lindi, that was the dream about the bakkie. I was not short of breath.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm hearing two different stories about the nights, so I won't settle that one now. Any dizziness?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh ja, when I stand up from the stoep chair the room goes a bit funny. Just for a moment.
[SEG0024] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She grabs the doorframe. Not every time. Most mornings.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any cough, or fever?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough. And I'm not hot. I checked, no fever.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Waterworks, bowels, anything there?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): All fine, regular, no burning. I eat too much pap sometimes but the tummy is okay. We had bobotie on Sunday, lekker.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Who sorts the pill box?
[SEG0030] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I do, every Sunday night. She can't read the small writing anymore.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): I take the little white one, and I also take the blood pressure tablet. Two different ones, doctor.
[SEG0032] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Ma'am, no. The little white one is the blood pressure tablet. It's the amlodipine. You've been counting it twice.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Is it? Ag. Then what about the one in the evening slot?

[SEG0034] person_3 (CAREGIVER): That's the thing. It's for the blood pressure. The dose on the blister is five milligrams... no, sorry, I looked again this morning, the blister says ten. Ten milligrams, one in the morning. But last week I found a second amlodipine in the evening slot. I think she popped an extra one in herself. I'm not sure how often.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): So one medicine, amlodipine ten milligrams, meant to be once in the morning, and some days there may have been a second one. I won't pretend we know how many extra.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): And the enalapril. I take twenty. The professor said twenty.
[SEG0037] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The box I have is ten milligrams, and ten is what goes in the box. She keeps saying twenty. I can't show you a twenty milligram packet because there isn't one.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): It was twenty. I'm sure. Or... no, I'm sure it was twenty.

[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then I can't record a dose for the enalapril. You're both certain and you don't match, and the packet isn't here. We'll leave the dose open. You are taking it every morning?

[SEG0040] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Most mornings. Some days she spits it into a tissue when it sticks in her throat. I don't know if it's two days a week or less. So I can't say she's taking it as it was written.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Noted. What about the water tablet?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): They stopped that. The other doctor, at the day hospital. The furosemide.
[SEG0043] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Furosemide forty milligrams. He stopped it. Said her kidneys, or the pressure was low, I can't remember which story.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): When was that stopped?
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Last winter. Or the winter before. After the cold snap, or was it before Easter? I can't put a date on it, doctor. My head doesn't keep dates.
[SEG0046] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I wasn't with her yet. No date in the folder either. The page is torn.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): I still take the Disprin for the heart. Seventy-five... no, no, the heart doctor changed it. A hundred and fifty. One in the morning, with water.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Aspirin one hundred and fifty milligrams each morning. Anything else in the box?
[SEG0049] person_3 (CAREGIVER): A yellow capsule at night, for the cholesterol. I don't know the name. The packet went out with the rubbish. It's just a yellow capsule, one at night. Smallish.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, the yellow one. Don't ask me the name. Looks like a little mielie pip.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any drug allergies? Penicillin, anything that disagreed with you?
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. I'm not allergic to any tablets.
[SEG0053] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Doctor, the old clinic card said penicillin. Her face came up in a rash. They told her daughter, who told me. She's avoided it since.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): That was the heat, not an allergy. I don't have allergies. I'm not agreeing to that.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll mark it as disputed, not as a clear allergy. Do you smoke, or take a drink?

[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Never smoked. My late husband smoked enough for both of us, shame. I have a sherry at Christmas and that's it. Hardly counts. We live together, Lindi and I, in the house in Parow.
[SEG0057] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She doesn't drink much at all, really. And she doesn't walk much anymore, just to the stoep.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): My father had a stroke, hey. Died at seventy. My mother was strong, she made the best koeksisters in the street.
[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any operations in the past?
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Nee, never been cut. Appendix and all still mine.
[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): And sugar diabetes?
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): No diabetes. They checked at the day hospital. Blood pressure, ja, that I've had for years and years. Since my sixties.

[SEG0063] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me look at the legs and listen to the chest. Ankles are puffy both sides, pitting up to the mid-shin. Chest is clear, I don't hear crackles. Heart sounds are regular, no murmur.

[SEG0064] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure sitting is one hundred and sixty-two over ninety-four millimetres of mercury. Pulse is seventy-six beats a minute. Oxygen saturation is ninety-seven percent on room air.

[SEG0065] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the swelling could be the amlodipine, it could be the heart not coping, it could just be the veins and the time on her feet. I'm not going to conclude heart failure today, and I don't want the blood test to do my thinking for me before I've said what I think. Let's see.

[SEG0066] person_1 (DOCTOR): With your longstanding high blood pressure, my working impression is that the ankle swelling is from the amlodipine. I still can't rule out a cardiac contribution, so that stays on the list, but I am not diagnosing heart failure.
[SEG0067] person_2 (PATIENT): So it's the little white one all along? And here I thought it was the bobotie salt.

[SEG0068] person_1 (DOCTOR): Salt doesn't help, but the change I'm making is the amlodipine. Stop it from today, don't put it in the box. In its place I'll start hydrochlorothiazide, twelve point five milligrams, one tablet by mouth in the morning. A small water tablet, not the furosemide they cancelled.
[SEG0069] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Twelve point five. Morning. By mouth. And the amlodipine goes out of the box. Ja, I'll do that.

[SEG0070] person_1 (DOCTOR): I also want kidney bloods, urea and electrolytes, today at the lab, and an ECG before you leave. If the swelling has not settled by the time I see you, we might then book a heart sonar, but not now.
[SEG0071] person_2 (PATIENT): The ECG stickers, they itch, hey. Last time the sister was rough.

[SEG0072] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in two weeks, with the yellow capsule if you find a stray packet, and with the enalapril box. If you get chest pain, or you can't get your breath, don't wait, go to casualty.
[SEG0073] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Two weeks. I'll bring whatever packets I can find. She'll moan about the stickers but she'll manage.
[SEG0074] person_2 (PATIENT): Can I still have rooibos with condensed milk? Lindi hides the sugar. Tell her it's fine, doctor. And the dog, really, you should hear him.

[SEG0075] person_1 (DOCTOR): Rooibos is fine. Go easy on the condensed milk and the salt, legs up on a cushion when you sit, and Lindi, one of each morning tablet only, no extras. Off you go, the ECG is down the passage.

Nobody can date when the other doctor stopped the furosemide.
The patient says the enalapril dose is 20 mg and the caregiver says the box is 10 mg, so no dose was recorded.
Amlodipine was meant to be one 10 mg tablet in the morning, but an extra tablet was sometimes in the evening slot and nobody knows how often.
The caregiver is not sure the enalapril is taken as written because some mornings the patient spits it out.
Neither the patient nor the caregiver can name the yellow capsule taken at night for cholesterol.
The patient denies waking short of breath at night and the caregiver says she sat up breathless on three nights this week.
The patient denies any tablet allergy while the caregiver recalls a penicillin rash on an old clinic card.

spec.situation: Older patient with a live-in carer or daughter who manages the pill box; names of tablets are described ('the little white one', 'the water tablet'), one was stopped by another doctor, one is double-counted. Doctor reviews and changes one medicine.
features: doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

bad.reason: Swollen ankles current, duration disputed; certainty 'certain' is wrong.
bad.text: swollen ankles (category=cardiovascular, status=present, duration=approximately 6 weeks to 2 months, temporality=current, body_site=ankles, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

omissions.text: Exertional shortness of breath is limited to walking to the gate/hill and not present inside the house.
The patient initially denied shortness of breath before later describing exertional breathlessness, so the symptom history was internally inconsistent.
Orthopnoea was denied: she sleeps flat with two pillows and no problem breathing at night by her own report.
Dizziness is brief/presyncopal only for a moment on standing, with caregiver adding that she grabs the doorframe and it happens not every time.
The patient denied paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea/night waking breathless, and this was specifically asked and answered, though disputed by the caregiver.
Enalapril was intended to be taken every morning, but actual adherence is only 'most mornings' because she sometimes spits it into a tissue when it sticks in her throat.
Amlodipine extra doses were suspected specifically as a second tablet placed in the evening slot by the patient, with unknown frequency.
The doctor explicitly stated he would not record an enalapril dose because the patient and caregiver disagreed and no packet was available.
The reason furosemide was stopped was uncertain between kidney concerns and low blood pressure.
Heart sounds were regular on examination.
